system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. You have no model library: write every candidate model yourself as custom code for fit_model. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms.
3. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
4. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
5. Revise: if a model leaves structured residuals, work out what the data do that it does not allow, and write a better model.
6. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
7. Submit with submit_model (mechanism_label 'custom'), citing fit_ids as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) and inhibitor concentrations I (uM). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 48 rows with columns: S, I, v. Your model will be used to predict rates at higher inhibitor concentrations.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Inspect data structure and per-group stats
Fit Michaelis-Menten baseline (I ignored) and competitive, uncompetitive, noncompetitive, mixed inhibition models
Compare BIC and residuals; check identifiability

steps: Inspect data structure and per-group stats

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
d=df.copy()
S=d.S.values; I=d.I.values; v=d.v.values
def fit(name,f,p0):
    best=None
    for s in range(30):
        p=np.array(p0)*np.exp(np.random.randn(len(p0))*0.7)
        r=least_squares(lambda q: f(q,S,I)-v, np.log(p), bounds=(-10,10))
        if best is None or r.cost<best.cost: best=r
    n=len(v);k=len(p0)+1;rss=2*best.cost
    aic=n*np.log(rss/n)+2*k; bic=n*np.log(rss/n)+k*np.log(n)
    print(name, np.round(np.exp(best.x),4), 'RSS',round(rss,4),'BIC',round(bic,2))
    return best
models={
 'MM':(lambda q,S,I: q[0]*S/(q[1]+S),[10,3]),
 'comp':(lambda q,S,I: q[0]*S/(q[1]*(1+I/q[2])+S),[10,3,1]),
 'uncomp':(lambda q,S,I: q[0]*S/(q[1]+S*(1+I/q[2])),[10,3,1]),
 'noncomp':(lambda q,S,I: q[0]*S/((q[1]+S)*(1+I/q[2])),[10,3,1]),
 'mixed':(lambda q,S,I: q[0]*S/(q[1]*(1+I/q[2])+S*(1+I/q[3])),[10,3,1,1]),
}
res={k:fit(k,f,p) for k,(f,p) in models.items()}
for k in res:
    pass
print(d.groupby(['I','S']).v.apply(lambda x: list(np.round(x,2))).unstack(0).to_string())

content.thinking:
The fitted Vmax came out around 22000, which looks wrong: that is exp(10), the upper edge of the log-parameter bound, so the optimizer pinned Vmax at its limit. Vmax seems unidentifiable here, with the fit diverging toward that bound.

The log-parameter objective is the culprit: I was passing the log values straight into the model without exponentiating them, so the fit never actually evaluated the intended parameters. Applying np.exp to q before computing the residuals should fix the diverging Vmax and the poor RSS.

content.text: The fitted parameters are hitting the bounds, which points to a bug: I passed log-parameters straight into the model without exponentiating. Refitting with that fixed.
